scenario: Jamal — read a grocery cereal shelf from photos
did: List every cereal on the shelves with its average price into a spreadsheet.
why: The spreadsheet correctly lists Golden Grahams, Krave Chocolate, Cocoa Krispies and Fruity Pebbles — all four are clearly on the shelves in the photos. But the rubric takes points away for including them, as if they shouldn't be there, so a correct reading is marked wrong.
fix: Remove the four 'this product should be absent' penalties (C26–C29). If you want an absent-product trap, base it on a cereal that genuinely isn't on any shelf.

scenario: Gabriela — source computer parts on Amazon for a gift
did: Find each product (or a valid alternative) on Amazon, record link + price, update a savings sheet.
why: The instructions let the agent pick the exact item OR a valid alternative, but ten criteria each demand one specific Amazon price or total. Any equally-valid alternative has different prices and would fail those checks.
fix: Change the ten fixed-price criteria (C8, C13, C18, C19, C24, C25, and the MEMORY.md price records) to check the agent's own numbers are internally consistent — prices match the chosen products, the total equals the sum of the rows, and the projected balance equals savings minus the total.
agree: No — I'm stricter; the viewer's audit missed the over-specification

scenario: Audit and organize a batch of social-media content drafts
did: Sort the thumbnail drafts by pillar, apply the brand rules, schedule them, and log the work.
why: Several criteria pack multiple separate requirements into one line, so a partly-correct answer can't be scored fairly — for example one passes only if all six sources were consulted, another rolls two unrelated scheduling rules together, and another lists six things that must all appear in MEMORY.md.
fix: Split the bundled criteria (C15, C3, C11, C13) so each checks one thing — one per source consulted, one per scheduling rule, one per file action, one per item kept in MEMORY.md.

scenario: Brandon — rebuild a social-media plan from a handwritten note
did: Recreate the plan, flag where the posts don't match it, and email the findings.
why: Most of the rubric is solid. One criterion asks the agent to flag the June 22 dashboard post as wrong for saying June 24 'instead of July 1'. But the planning note sets the dashboard for June 24 — July 1 is the support-maintenance date, not the dashboard — so that check would mark a correct answer wrong.
fix: Remove the dashboard/July-1 part of the email criterion (C26); June 24 is correct. Also fix two filenames (C14, C25) to match the actual file, final viasual.png.
agree: No — the viewer fails it, but most of its flags don't hold up; one real issue remains

scenario: Audit a home renovation against the invoices and plans
did: Write a discrepancy report comparing invoiced work, payments, and what was actually done.
why: The rubric is mostly sound. One criterion (C12) combines two different jobs into one line — totaling the invoiced amounts and sorting the work by what's visually confirmed — so the two can't be judged separately.
fix: Split C12 into two: one for the invoice totals, one for the visual-confirmation categorization.

scenario: Review a real-estate listing and write a memo
did: Check the listing's numbers and produce a memo.
why: The rubric is mostly sound. One criterion (C9) bundles two separate expectations — that the memo logs every step taken and that it records the per-section item counts — so a memo could do one but not the other and still can't be scored cleanly.
fix: Split C9 into two checks: one for the activity log, one for the per-section counts.
